$comment: What each fixture isolates, and what the Resolver must get right about it. Written before the Resolver exists, so it reads as a specification rather than a description of whatever the extractor happens to do.

design.handWritten: Not sampled from a real repository. The Phase A corpus was two JHipster-generated components, and generated code is far more regular than hand-written code -- schema fields derived from it inherit that bias (3_PhaseAFindings.md F5a). These are written to isolate one construct each instead.
design.pairs: Fixtures come in pairs that express the SAME semantics in different syntax. The pair is the assertion: both members must extract to equivalent output, differing only in the field that records which syntax was used. This is the check that catches D3's silent-failure mode -- a regex-based extractor tends to handle one member of a pair and quietly mis-handle the other, producing confidently wrong metadata rather than an error.
design.equivalence: Pairs are compared by SEMANTIC PROJECTION, not by diffing fields. Two different source files differ in array order, ids, line numbers and expression text for reasons that say nothing about whether they were read equivalently, so a field diff is mostly noise -- and quieting noise is how a first attempt ended up deriving its own expectations from the output it was judging. Each projection answers a question mustExtract already asks in prose, and those assertions predate the extractor, which is what makes them a specification. Anything a pair may legitimately differ on is named as a projection with a reason. A pair that cannot be field-compared at all is marked assertions-only and REPORTED AS UNCHECKED -- never as passing.

fixtures.isolates: How the public API is declared: @Input/@Output decorators versus the input()/output()/model() functions.
mustExtract: three inputs in both members, named label, count, internalName
count is required in both -- via the decorator option in one, input.required in the other
internalName carries alias 'aliasedName' in both
one output named changed with payload type number
declarationStyle is the ONLY field that may differ: 'decorator' versus 'signal'
the signal member additionally declares model:selected, which has no decorator equivalent

equivalence.reason: model() has no decorator equivalent, so the signal member declares one extra two-way binding. Everything else -- names, requiredness, aliases, the output payload -- must match.

fixtures.isolates: How dependencies are injected: constructor parameters versus inject() field initializers.
mustExtract: three dependencies in both, named http, route, cache
visibility preserved: http private, route protected, cache private
cache carries optional and skipSelf modifiers in both -- as parameter decorators in one, as an options object in the other
resolvedUnitId is null for the two Angular tokens and non-null for CacheService
injectionStyle is the only field that may differ
the inject() member's dependencies are field initializers, so their loc is a field, not a constructor parameter

equivalence.reason: Syntax-only in both directions: same three dependencies, same tokens, same visibility, same optional/skipSelf modifiers. Nothing may differ.

fixtures.isolates: Template control flow: structural directives (*ngIf/*ngFor/ngSwitch) versus block syntax (@if/@for/@switch).
mustExtract: one conditional, one loop, one switch with two cases, in both
the loop's track expression: trackBy function in one, track item.id in the other
the index alias in both
the else branch in both -- an ng-template reference in one, an @else block in the other
the block member additionally declares an @empty branch, which has no structural-directive equivalent
the uppercase pipe recorded once per member
construct is the only field that may differ
the structural member reaches method:trackById from the template (trackBy binding) and reports it NOT unreachable; the block member reports it unreachable, because `track item.id` calls nothing

equivalence.reason: @else is a branch record while the structural form expresses it as a separate ng-template, and @empty has no structural equivalent -- so branch counts differ. trackBy: fn versus track item.id differ in kind. Structural directives need a host element, so ng-container appears where a block needs none. The primary constructs -- one conditional, one loop, one switch -- must match exactly. `unreachable` differs as a CONSEQUENCE of that trackBy difference, not independently: the structural member binds trackBy: trackById so the template reaches the method, while the block member's `track item.id` reaches nothing, leaving trackById genuinely uncalled there. Expect exactly one entry either way -- empty on both members would mean reachability stopped being computed, not that the two agree.

fixtures.isolates: Form construction: FormBuilder groups versus ngModel bindings.
mustExtract: approach is 'reactive' versus 'template-driven'
an email control with required and email validators in both
the reactive member's id control is disabled AND required -- the required rule is inert because disabled controls skip validation, and this must be visible in the output rather than collapsed
getRawValue() is recorded distinctly from value(): it includes disabled controls, which is load-bearing
the template-driven member has no form group id, so form:<name> ids are absent rather than invented

equivalence.note: these members differ in MECHANISM, not syntax: one builds a FormGroup in TypeScript, the other annotates a template, so almost nothing lines up structurally. Mechanising this needs a normalised form model both project into, which does not exist. The pair still earns its place -- it caught approach reporting 'none' instead of 'template-driven' -- but by reading, not by diffing.

fixtures.isolates: Subscription teardown: takeUntilDestroyed versus a Subscription field unsubscribed in ngOnDestroy.
mustExtract: cleanupStrategy is 'takeUntilDestroyed' versus 'ngOnDestroy-unsubscribe'
leakRisk is 'none' for both -- neither leaks, by different means
the manual member implements OnDestroy and the other does not
the rxjs operator chain in both: map, plus takeUntilDestroyed in the first
an extractor that equates 'has ngOnDestroy' with 'safe' would pass the manual member and wrongly flag the other

equivalence.reason: The two mechanisms genuinely require different members: one injects DestroyRef, the other holds a Subscription and implements OnDestroy. What must NOT differ is leakRisk -- neither leaks, by different means -- and that is the assertion the pair exists to make.

fixtures.isolates: An ICU plural expression -- deliberately a construct the walker does NOT handle. This fixture asserts the GAP IS REPORTED, not that ICU is extracted.
mustExtract: the interpolation of `label` in the sibling span, proving the walker keeps working past the node it cannot handle
parse.nodesUnrecognized is 1, counting nodes THIS walker did not record
provenance.parseStatus is 'partial', derived from the warning rather than asserted
one unhandled-template-node warning naming TmplAstIcu
the ICU content itself is absent from ast -- recorded nowhere, which is honest, because guessing at pluralisation rules would be worse

equivalence.reason: Single-member fixture: there is no second syntax for an ICU expression, so there is nothing to pair it against. It earns its place as a regression test for the detector rather than as a syntax-equivalence pair (F10a).

fixtures.isolates: Where the template lives: an inline `template:` literal versus a `templateUrl` whose filename deliberately does not match the .ts stem.
mustExtract: both members extract the SAME UI: one @if, one click event bound to method:toggle, one interpolation of title
the inline member's locs resolve into the .ts and are offset by the template literal's own line -- not line 1
the external member resolves ./panel-markup.html from the DECORATOR, not from the .ts stem
unit.files.templateInline distinguishes them and is the only field that may differ besides file names and line numbers
neither member raises template-not-found
both members record the same ast.staticText -- the words on the screen do not depend on where the template is stored (F19)

equivalence.reason: The pair exists to prove template LOCATION does not change what is extracted. templateFile names two different files and templateInline records which mechanism was used; both must be non-null/boolean rather than merely absent, so an extractor that produced nothing for one member cannot satisfy this.

fixtures.isolates: A declared templateUrl that does not resolve. Asserts the GAP IS REPORTED, not that a template is extracted.
mustExtract: provenance.parseStatus is 'partial'
exactly one template-not-found warning, naming the declared url
no template.json is produced -- and that absence is accompanied by the warning, never silent
signature still extracts fully: one unreachable declaration must not cost the rest of the unit

equivalence.reason: Single-member: 'declared but missing' has no equivalent second syntax. It earns its place as a regression test for the distinction between a missing template and an absent one.

fixtures.isolates: Event handlers that are not a bare call at position 0 -- guarded by an expression, preceded by another call, or two calls chained.
mustExtract: five event bindings, one per button
`items.length && save()` records handlerMethod method:save -- an expression guard does not hide the call
`$event.stopPropagation(); close()` records method:close -- a preceding call on something else does not hide it
`reset(); save()` records method:reset as the primary handler and warns that a second component method is called
`items.join('save')` records handlerMethod null -- a string argument that happens to name a method is NOT a call
every recorded handlerMethod appears as a template caller in the call graph, so none of save/close/reset is reported unreachable

equivalence.reason: Single-member: these are five variants of one construct rather than two syntaxes for one semantic, so there is nothing to pair against. It earns its place because each variant was a distinct silent miss.

fixtures.isolates: Reactive control shapes whose meaning text matching read wrongly: a computed `disabled`, an `updateOn` option, a builder-made array, and a string literal that names both.
mustExtract: five controls: title, note, slow, tags, hint
note.disabledExpression is the EXPRESSION `this.locked`, not a boolean and not null -- a computed disabled state is still a disabled state
slow.updateOn is 'blur' -- read from the options object rather than hardcoded null
tags.type is 'array', from fb.array(...) rather than from the substring FormArray
hint is type 'control' with disabledExpression null -- the string mentioning 'disabled: true and FormArray' must contribute NOTHING
title records exactly the validators required and maxLength

equivalence.reason: Single-member: the point is that one syntax is read correctly, not that two syntaxes agree. hint is the load-bearing case -- it is the control that text matching got wrong in two fields at once.

fixtures.isolates: outputFromObservable -- an output driven by a stream rather than emitted from code.
mustExtract: one output named tick with declarationStyle 'outputFromObservable'
emittedFrom names stream:ticks$, linking the public contract to the stream that drives it
stream:ticks$ resolves -- it is declared in stateOutline.streamIds, so the link is not dangling
the output is NOT recorded as output-fn or subject: the mechanism differs and so does its teardown story

equivalence.reason: Single-member: outputFromObservable has no equivalent in the decorator or output() styles -- an output fed by a stream is a different mechanism, not different syntax for the same one. That is why it needed its own declarationStyle rather than being folded into an existing value.

notCoveredYet.$comment: Named so their absence is a decision rather than an oversight. Each is a construct the Phase A corpus exercised or the taxonomy names, with no fixture yet.
constructs: ViewChild/ContentChild queries, decorator and signal forms
inherited members from a base class -- the extensionPoints case (F5a)
cross-component shared mutable service state, which is the highest-severity migration risk and not observable from one unit (F3)
ICU expressions themselves -- fixtures/i18n-icu asserts the gap is REPORTED, not that it is extracted
async validators, and cross-field (group-level) validators -- neither fixture exercises them
